transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, I'm Tracey, a 70-year-old retiree, and I’m constantly forgetting little everyday things—appointments, errands, even finishing what I start for the community center. My husband and friends were actually starting to worry that I might be developing early dementia. However, my primary care doctor suggested that it might actually be a long-standing attention issue instead, which is why I'm here.
Can you tell me when you first started noticing these difficulties with memory and attention, was it something that began recently or has it been a problem for you throughout your life?

These problems have really interfered with my life over the last two years since I retired, but looking back, I've struggled with attention my whole life. Even in elementary school, my report cards said I was bright but daydreamed and talked out of turn, and I'd always leave my chores half-done. I managed to compensate during my working years with a lot of structure, but losing that routine has really exposed these long-standing issues.
Did you also experience excessive restlessness, fidgeting, or an inability to sit still, especially during your childhood and teenage years?

Yes, I absolutely did. As a child, my mother always scolded me for wandering off halfway through my chores, and I've always struggled with a pent-up urge to get up and move. Even now, I find myself constantly tapping my foot or fiddling with my jewelry when I'm supposed to be sitting quietly in church or book club.
Have you ever acted on impulse without much consideration for the consequences, such as interrupting others, blurting out answers, or doing things that might be risky or inappropriate?

Yes, I definitely do that, especially during committee meetings at the community center where I'll jump in to finish other people's sentences or blurt out my ideas before they're done talking. I usually only realize afterward that I've cut them off again. This isn't a new thing either, as even my elementary school report cards always mentioned that I talked out of turn.
Can you think of any situations where you've had difficulty waiting for your turn, such as in line or during conversations, and how have you handled those situations over the years?

When I'm waiting in lines, like at the pharmacy or the community center, I get incredibly impatient, constantly check the time, and literally have to bite my tongue to keep from nudging things along. In conversations, I still catch myself jumping in to finish other people's sentences or blurting out my ideas before they can even finish. I've tried to handle it over the years by consciously forcing myself to wait, but it takes a lot of mental effort and I still slip up quite a bit.

You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you tell me more about how they affected you during your teenage and young adult years, before you established your career and daily routines?

To be honest, I don't recall many specific struggles or details from my teenage and young adult years. I think I managed to get by well enough back then, so those memories aren't nearly as clear to me as my childhood report cards or the difficulties I'm facing now.

You've described a lifelong pattern of struggles with attention and impulsivity, but can you clarify if these symptoms have remained relatively consistent over the years or if you've noticed any significant changes, especially considering your recent retirement and the concerns about dementia?

I've had these tendencies my whole life, but I compensated for them for decades using strict daily routines. Since retiring and losing that structure about two years ago, these attention and organization issues have become much more visible and disruptive. While my family worried about dementia, my memory for conversations and stories is actually fine—it's just my ability to organize, focus, and track details that has broken down.
Have you experienced any symptoms of hyperactivity, such as feeling restless or having trouble engaging in quiet leisure activities, in addition to your difficulties with attention and impulsivity?

Yes, I definitely feel a pent-up energy during quiet movie nights or long talks, and I often have to get up to straighten chairs or wash dishes just to move. I also really struggle with quiet activities like reading on the porch or doing yoga, because being still feels so uncomfortable that I quickly start humming, talking, or getting up to start a project.
You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you confirm if you experienced significant symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity before the age of 12?

Yes, I definitely experienced those symptoms before age 12. Back in elementary school, my teachers always wrote on my report cards that I was bright but "daydreams, rushes, and talks out of turn." My mother also used to scold me constantly for never finishing my chores because I’d wander off halfway through to do something else.
Can you confirm if you experienced significant symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity before the age of 7, and have these symptoms persisted consistently throughout your life?

Yes, those behaviors were definitely present even before age seven, as my mother always scolded me for leaving chores unfinished and my earliest school reports noted I rushed and daydreamed. These patterns persisted throughout my life, but I managed to compensate for them through the highly structured routines of my working years. It is only since retiring and losing that external structure that they have become a major problem for me again.

To confirm, you're saying that these symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity have not only been present since before age 7 but have also persisted in some form throughout your entire life, correct?

Yes, that is absolutely correct. Looking back, these issues have been present since my early childhood, like when my mother would scold me for unfinished chores or my teachers wrote about me daydreaming and talking out of turn. I managed to compensate for these difficulties during my working years by relying on very strict routines, but they have resurfaced and become much more noticeable since I retired.
Have you experienced significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning as a result of these symptoms, and if so, can you give me some specific examples?

Yes, it's been quite embarrassing, but I've really started letting people down at the community center by forgetting supply runs, mixing up dates, and missing important tasks. It has gotten to the point where a few volunteers have even gently suggested I step back from leading certain projects because they are worried things will fall through the cracks.

Can you describe how your symptoms of hyperactivity, such as restlessness or feeling fidgety, have impacted your daily life and relationships, particularly in situations where you're expected to remain still or quiet?

When I'm in church or book club, I constantly tap my foot or fiddle with my bracelet, and I worry it's distracting to the people next to me. During quiet movie nights, I get this pent-up energy that makes me want to jump up and wash dishes or straighten things, to the point where my family jokes that I never just sit down and relax. It really makes quiet, still moments feel uncomfortable and stressful for me.

You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood and have persisted throughout your life, but can you think of any period, even a short one, where you didn't experience any of these symptoms, or have they been consistently present?

No, they have been consistently present throughout my life without any breaks. They were just much easier to manage during my working years because of the strict routines and structure I had in place. Once I retired and lost that structure about two years ago, the struggles became highly visible and disruptive again, but they never actually went away.

Can you describe any situations where you've been able to control or significantly reduce your hyperactive behaviors, such as restlessness or fidgeting, and what strategies you used to achieve that control?

I really struggle to control or reduce those feelings of restlessness and fidgeting. While I try to catch myself and force myself to stop—like reminding myself to stop tapping my foot or fiddling with my bracelet in church—it is incredibly difficult to sustain. I haven't really found any effective strategies that successfully quiet down that inner restlessness or stop my constant need to be on the go.
Have you experienced any significant periods of remission or improvement in your symptoms, particularly during adulthood, or have they consistently impacted your daily life and relationships?

I wouldn't say I had periods of remission, but rather my symptoms were long-compensated during my adulthood by the highly structured routine of my full-time work and a household manager setup. It was only after retiring about two years ago and losing that external structure that these attention difficulties truly surfaced. Since then, they have consistently impacted my daily life and my ability to manage things at the community center.

Can you tell me if you have experienced any significant changes in your symptoms, such as a notable decrease in hyperactivity with age, which might help differentiate between the possible diagnoses we are considering?

I'm not really sure if it has decreased, as I haven't thought about it in terms of a change. I still feel incredibly restless and am constantly on the go, so it doesn't feel like that inner energy has quieted down much at all.
